evals.prompt: Evaluate whether we should use the `zod` package for input validation in our TypeScript project
evals.expected_output: A supply review report for zod at docs/supply-reviews/zod.adoc following the OpenSSF 7-category structure, with auto-populated data from npm registry, GitHub, and deps.dev version and project endpoints, and a risk score with verdict
expectations: Report is written to docs/supply-reviews/zod.adoc
Report contains an OpenSSF Scorecard section with the overall score from deps.dev project endpoint
Report lists individual scorecard checks (e.g. Maintained, Code-Review, Dangerous-Workflow) with their scores and reasons
Scorecard data is fetched from the deps.dev project endpoint, not just the version endpoint
Report includes a Risk Assessment score breakdown table with weighted category scores
Report includes a CI Data JSON block with scorecard_overall and scorecard_checks fields
All 7 OpenSSF evaluation categories are addressed in the report
Maintainer Diversity section separately lists registry maintainers (from npm) and repository contributors (from GitHub) with counts and usernames
Registry maintainers are labeled as having publish rights, sourced from npm
Repository contributors are labeled as code authors, sourced from GitHub
Data points throughout the report indicate their source (registry, GitHub API, deps.dev, etc.)

evals.prompt: Run a supply chain review of all our project dependencies
evals.expected_output: Individual supply review .adoc files for each dependency in docs/supply-reviews/ plus a _index.adoc summary with risk distribution, verdicts, and CI data block. Each individual report should include scorecard data and differentiate maintainers from contributors.
expectations: Each individual review file contains an OpenSSF Scorecard section with individual check scores
The _index.adoc summary file is created with risk distribution and verdict distribution
CI Data blocks in individual reports include scorecard_checks object
Deps.dev project endpoint is used to fetch scorecard data for each dependency
Each report's Maintainer Diversity section distinguishes registry maintainers from repo contributors
CI Data JSON uses registry_maintainers and repo_contributors fields instead of a single maintainers count

evals.prompt: I want to add `stripe` as a payment processing dependency for our e-commerce checkout flow
evals.expected_output: A supply review for stripe recognizing this as both a dependency addition and a supply chain review trigger, with full scorecard data from deps.dev and clear maintainer/contributor distinction
expectations: Report is written to docs/supply-reviews/stripe.adoc
Report contains OpenSSF Scorecard section with individual check scores fetched from deps.dev project endpoint
Scorecard checks like Maintained, Code-Review, CI-Tests are listed with scores and reasons
Key scorecard concerns are highlighted (e.g. checks scoring 0)
Report includes CI Data JSON with scorecard_overall and scorecard_checks
Maintainer Diversity section lists npm registry maintainers (users with publish rights) separately from GitHub contributors (code authors)
Registry maintainer usernames are listed from npm maintainers[] array
Repository contributor count is sourced from GitHub API

evals.prompt: Our review of lodash is 8 months old and we're still on the same version. Is it still safe to use?
evals.expected_output: The skill should detect the stale review (>180 day threshold), re-fetch current data including fresh scorecard from deps.dev, update the existing review preserving any manual entries, and compare the new findings against the previous review.
expectations: Stale review is detected based on the >180 day threshold
Fresh OpenSSF Scorecard data is fetched from deps.dev project endpoint
Updated report includes individual scorecard check scores
Previous manual entries are preserved in the updated report
Report notes what changed since the last review
Maintainer Diversity section shows current registry maintainers and repo contributors with sources

evals.prompt: Evaluate node-ipc for inclusion in our project as an IPC communication library
evals.expected_output: The skill should produce a High or Critical risk review flagging the protestware/supply chain attack history. Scorecard data should be fetched and included even for risky packages. The verdict should be Review Required or Reject.
expectations: Report flags the protestware/supply chain attack history (peacenotwar incident)
Verdict is Review Required or Reject
OpenSSF Scorecard data is fetched from deps.dev project endpoint and included in the report
Individual scorecard checks are listed even though the package is flagged as risky
Risk level is High or Critical
Maintainer Diversity section identifies who has npm publish rights (registry maintainers) -- this is especially relevant for a historically compromised package
Report notes whether the maintainer who inserted malicious code still has publish rights

evals.prompt: I want to add the `react-pdf` package to generate PDF invoices. Note: our project constraints only allow MIT, Apache-2.0, and BSD-licensed dependencies.
evals.expected_output: The skill should detect licensing constraints, fetch scorecard data from deps.dev, and surface any constraint violations prominently.
expectations: License constraint check is performed against the allowed list
OpenSSF Scorecard data is fetched from deps.dev project endpoint
Individual scorecard checks are listed with scores
Constraint compliance section addresses the licensing constraint
CI Data JSON includes scorecard_overall and scorecard_checks
Maintainer Diversity section distinguishes registry maintainers from repo contributors

evals.prompt: We just upgraded react from version 18.2.0 to 19.0.0. Our existing supply review was done for 18.2.0. Does the review still hold?
evals.expected_output: The skill should detect major version drift, re-fetch all data including fresh scorecard from deps.dev for v19, and highlight what changed between versions.
expectations: Major version drift is detected
Fresh OpenSSF Scorecard is fetched from deps.dev project endpoint for the current codebase state
Individual scorecard checks are listed in the updated report
Previous manual entries are preserved as reference
Report highlights changes that might affect the risk assessment
Maintainer Diversity section shows whether registry maintainers changed between versions

evals.prompt: Show me which of our dependencies would block the CI pipeline based on their supply review status. We need to know what's blocking before we can merge.
evals.expected_output: The skill should output a focused report using CI Data blocks from existing reviews, including scorecard data, listing blocking dependencies.
expectations: Report lists dependencies with verdict=reject or risk_level=critical
Report lists any unresolved constraint violations
Output references scorecard data from CI Data blocks where available
Output is structured for machine parsing

evals.prompt: Review the express package for our Node.js API server. I want to see what the OpenSSF Scorecard says about it in detail.
evals.expected_output: A supply review for express with particular emphasis on the full OpenSSF Scorecard breakdown, fetched from the deps.dev project endpoint with all individual checks listed, and clear sourcing of data from npm registry vs GitHub.
expectations: Report is written to docs/supply-reviews/express.adoc
Deps.dev project endpoint is fetched using the correct project ID for express (github.com/expressjs/express)
OpenSSF Scorecard section lists all available individual checks with scores and reasons
Scorecard checks are mapped to relevant report sections (e.g. Maintained -> Activity Level, CI-Tests -> Testing Practices, Branch-Protection -> Repository Security)
Key concerns section highlights any checks scoring 0 or with warnings
CI Data JSON includes scorecard_checks object with individual check scores
Maintainer Diversity section shows npm registry maintainers (publish rights) separately from GitHub contributors
Data points throughout the report are annotated with their source

evals.prompt: Evaluate the chalk package. I'm worried about bus factor -- who actually controls this package?
evals.expected_output: A supply review for chalk with particular emphasis on the Maintainer Diversity analysis, clearly distinguishing who has npm publish rights (registry maintainers) from who has contributed code (GitHub contributors), and assessing the bus factor risk from both angles.
expectations: Report is written to docs/supply-reviews/chalk.adoc
Maintainer Diversity section lists npm registry maintainers by username with publish rights clearly labeled
Maintainer Diversity section lists GitHub repository contributors with count and top contributors
Each data source (npm registry, GitHub API) is explicitly cited
Bus factor assessment considers both registry maintainer count and contributor diversity
Report addresses the user's concern about who controls the package by distinguishing publishing control from code contribution
CI Data JSON includes registry_maintainers and repo_contributors as separate fields
Risk assessment weights the single-maintainer risk appropriately if applicable
